This necessitates not only more action, but a better, faster, and more coherent global humanitarian response from the organization to meet these increasing demands. We take note of the ambitious new humanitarian compact under the UNAD framework aimed at maximizing impact through strengthening deficiency, coherence, and operational effectiveness. We see merit in the streamlining of humanitarian needs and response plans as shorter and sharper planning instruments as envisaged under the humanitarian reset can reduce administrative burden and redirect energy towards delivery and actual impact on the ground. However, this must not come at the expense of inclusivity and national ownership. Host governments must remain central to needs assessments, prioritization, and implementation frameworks. In addition, no matter how coherent and efficient the humanitarian response is, it must be funded through more predictable and sustainable funding streams. Hence, efficiency gains would translate into significant savings that could mean additional resources. We believe that regional procurement and increased reliance on local vendors would contribute greatly to this effect. We underline the importance of action 21 on collaborative humanitarian diplomacy under the coordination of the emergency relief coordinator at a time when humanitarian access is increasingly constrained at times even deliberately under attack, strengthened and coherent diplomatic advocacy in defense of humanitarian principles and international humanitarian law is indispensable. Such efforts must remain grounded in neutrality, impartiality, and independence while respecting sovereignty and territorial integrity. Lastly, I would like to underscore the importance of these briefings in keeping Member States updated on the developments on Workstream 3, given the complexity and enormity of this undertaking. To the interveners, I want to thank everybody to just keep the introductions and statements within the time frame. That's a sign of respect to all the colleagues and I hope that we can put this rule trend in the General Assembly Hall. So now I invite Mr Tom Fletcher to provide observations on the interventions made by delegations. Mr Fletcher, you have the floor.

Many thanks indeed and thank you colleagues for such an excellent set of feedback and questions. And thank you to Romania and others for recognizing the energy that we certainly feel as a collective group and to many of you for recognizing the way that we are operating as that single unit as we pioneer these reforms. I will leave Ted, Matthew, Kelly maybe to come in on supply chains and procurement where they have done more work than anyone on the detail of that. I've picked up four things which I'll touch on that you've raised. Firstly, we had a number of questions around the overlap, the alignment between the humanitarian reset, which is an exercise led across the IASC and as Norway and others recognized, predated UNAT and of course the new humanitarian compact which is a centerpiece of UNAT and I heard and noted the concerns from the US and Russia and others on the nomenclature of the compact. Some big themes which are part of the reset but also apply to UNAT. One is the increase in focus on pooled funds. The EU started with this. My personal target is to get half of funding through pooled funds and to make sure that 70% of that funding moves to local organizations. But we're a long way from that. And the sector is moving in that direction, but we've got to be careful to move at the right pace. We've just recently had a big US investment in the pooled funds, which is helping us in that direction. Second big part of the reset that several mentioned is empowering HC's. I heard this in the EU from Sweden, Ireland and many others. Vital, vital part of this exercise. And I would argue a vital part of UNAT more broadly. I think we need really strong empowered country representatives, whether they're HC's or HC's and RC's or just RC's. And I've just come from South Sudan where we have an outstanding humanitarian coordinator. Another big theme is localization mentioned by Belgium, Norway, many others. You asked how do we support localization? One way is to increase the authority of humanitarian country teams and humanitarian coordinators. And we're doing that through increasing the amount of money that goes through the pooled funds. Another way, and we've seen a lot of change in the last six months, is to get more local organizations onto those country teams. not just as add-ons, an extra meeting at the end of the main gathering, but actually in the room helping to make those decisions about funding. We're getting more local organizations onto the IASC principles group. And our next meeting, we've decided we'll have that expanded engagement. And again, back to the pooled funds, the more money that's going through the pooled funds, the more you empower local organizations. 100% of our last Sudan allocation went to local organizations. the last 60 percent over half of all the pooled fund allocations have gone to local organizations. This is tangible, tangible change. Also for the reset, a number of people mentioned the importance of planning prioritization and that's why we've put so much emphasis on the global humanitarian overview which I launched in December based on data and expertise from the field. Lichtenstein and others mentioned the importance of that. And finally on the reset, several said, this cannot be a technocratic exercise. The same applies to UNAT, of course. It's going to be about reimagination. And that's why I welcome the question from Australia on artificial intelligence. For me, that means making sure the algorithm is more humanitarian than humans. It means an emphasis on multipurpose cash, on responding to the consequences of climate shocks. And I'm grateful to so many countries in the room, member states in the room, for backing the emergency fund. Reimagination and innovation cannot just be top down. It's about encouraging risk, encouraging the space for innovation. Second big theme you raised is around what we famously call the nexus between humanitarian and development work. Norway, UK and others raised this. It gives me a chance to mention the strategic platform initiative that Amina Mohamed as DSG and I are co-chairing, which is looking at common appraisals. actually quite a radical change within the UN. Common services across not just humanitarians, but beyond into the development partners, common locations. As part of this, several people mentioned OCHA DCO and OCHA HCR coordination. As part of this, more OCHA and DCO offices will be co-located. We have a big focus on that. I think Germany raised that point. And of course, the more you build up HC's, the more you build up RC's, and these are of course the same person. And so building up those individuals is a great way to ensure that synergy. Thirdly, humanitarian diplomacy raised by Australia, the EU, many others. This isn't, we're not inventing something new here. So to give you three examples from this week, I was doing humanitarian diplomacy in South Sudan on Monday, which opened up new access routes to Jonglei across the fighting. And we got convoys through today of lifesaving food. I was doing Humanitarian Diplomacy Day on the Kordofans, trying to get us access to areas that are cut off. And Humanitarian Diplomacy Day on Goma, trying to get us more protection. Humanitarian diplomacy is also about trying to get the NGOs access to Gaza, for example. And it's about making sure that we coordinate our visits among humanitarian leaders. So we're not all going to Sudan in the same month, and we're not neglecting other crucial crises. We're doing it in two ways. And I really believe we should not create some huge, great new cross UN, across member state, across UN humanitarian agency mechanism on this. We have a working level group for exchanging information among the agencies. And I chair a principals meeting every couple of weeks where we discuss the overall strategy to our humanitarian diplomacy. Finally, a number of member states raised issues around funding and accountability, key, key questions. And in a way, These constitute, I suppose, more than anything else, our asks of you as Member States. So, the Russian Federation mentioned donor demands increasing. Absolutely, we recognize why so many Member States are looking for more accountability in the system to their taxpayers for the generosity of the funding that we get, but these can be incredibly onerous. The more that we harmonize and simplify your demands of us, the more money we can direct to saving lives. I hope that our new accountability and impact teams will be one great way of doing that. Many of you raised Brazil's point about outcomes being essential. I completely agree. Efficiency only matters if it helps us save more lives. And we are going out there this year to save 87 million lives as part of this hyper-prioritized plan that's more than died in the Second World War. And what we're asking for that is $23 billion, less than 1% of what you will be spending collectively on guns and arms this year. So we need you to get behind us. I'm very grateful to the EU, the US, Germany, Netherlands, Switzerland, and others who have already committed significant billion plus pledges to that hyper prioritized plan this year with others I know on the way. I do stress, though, that alongside pooled funding, we need funding for direct core funding for the agencies. And as Germany and others mentioned, the gold standard remains unearmarked multi-year funding. That is what we most ask for. And I note the commentary from many on the funding cuts that we face, and thank you for recognizing those funding cuts. I feel duty bound to not put that in the passive tense though. These are funding cuts by member states. These are not funding cuts happening outside beyond that. Irish colleague asked what more could you all do then? And the answer is please fund this plan, fund the programs and get behind the priorities that you've asked us to set. Just to close, I'm really grateful to you all for the clear support for the reset and the compact. Most of all, I'm very, very grateful for the unequivocal backing for principled, neutral, humanitarian action. These aren't just words. Really matters right now when our work is under such sustained attack. So thank you for that. Thank you for backing us on IHL. Thank you, Spain, the UK, and others who mentioned the importance of protecting work to protect women and girls. We are absolutely doubling down on that work, as I reassured our excellent colleagues on the UNFPA board last week. And thank you to Australia and others for their mention of the importance of protection of humanitarian workers. Please hold those to account who are killing us. Please don't kill us. And please think very carefully about arming those who are killing us. We'd be delighted to offer further briefings on data, on the timelines, on supply chains, on other details. But We really value this interactive session with you. We have lots of ideas to take away and we look forward to working with you in the spirit of close partnership to deliver genuine change swiftly that saves as many lives as we can. Thank you.
I thank Mr. Fletcher for extensive responding to the delegation's questions and now invite Ms. Michelle Giles-McDonough to reply to the observations of the delegations.

Thank you, Mr. President, for giving me the floor, and I thank Member States for the important questions and the feedback, and for the opportunity to respond on Work Package 17. This has been a very important opportunity for us to hear Member States' expectations. There was one issue raised around action 72, which is the joint mechanism linking the research and training pillar that was raised by Australia, wanting to clarify UN entities that would fall under this action and to be assured that there would not be multiplication of mechanisms. And I just wanted to respond that there is a thorough mapping that is underway of all institutions and their work in training and research so that we have a comprehensive picture to take into the design of this joint mechanism. And that for the mechanism, we're prioritizing using existing infrastructure and doing everything not to create any new infrastructure, but just to ensure that we have a way to articulate and have a close loop between research, training, and action in the field. In terms of the merger, There are five main issues that were raised and before I go into that, I just want to assure because a number of Member States spoke to the need for transparent and inclusive consultations and also for timely information and I just wanted to assure that this has been prioritized and we will As the analytical process unfolds and more information becomes available, we will be in touch with US member states as well as with our respective boards and also bringing our staff, our colleagues along with us. In terms of the five issues, the first was a caution against an approach that was focusing on structures. And I wanna say here that we welcome the priority that member states placed in this discussion on putting priority on the core purpose and function rather than structure and the guidance given in this direction. In this regard, this is why we have taken an approach of a strategic design. aimed at maximising coherence, efficiency and impact, and in agreeing around the value to be created by undergoing such a merger. This has been our starting point and then to ensure that that frames the analytical process that is now unfolding. There is another issue around programme continuity for both the staff college and UNITAR. I also want to state here that the work of both entities is continuing unimpeded. Both institutions have clear strategies and annual goals, targets and related implementation plans. Work flow and deliverables are being monitored as per normal. Work continues as per normal while we work through this merger. There were questions around the future funding model, operating model and governance infrastructure that would be put in place. At this stage, it is too early to provide information on this. This is why we have structured the analysis in three phases. The first phase is an as-is phase, understanding what each institution is in order to inform future state options going forward. As we complete the analytical phase at the end of March, we will be in a better position to think about in what direction it leads us on funding, operating models and governance. There was an issue raised also about transition risks. And I also just want to say built into the analytical framework is a clear focus around analyzing transition risks and then looking forward at risk at mitigation measures toward designing also a transition plan that would be appropriate for day one readiness. And the final issue raised was around preserving local campus ecosystems raised by Germany, Italy, and Switzerland. And just to note the importance of that the full analysis will be conducted with a view to delivering the value foreseen in a single coherent learning engine. We will follow a rigorous approach to inform these future state options. And we're well aware of the value these different campus locations bring and how important they are in terms of the research to action interface that is vital to the work we deliver. And so as the analysis unfolds, we will keep all member states updated. Finally, the point around in delivering the services of this new learning engine that we keep geographic representation in clear view. And just to assure this has long been the practice of our entities, both geographic and gender representation are already a central focus and they will continue through to this merged entity proposal that we will provide. I want to thank Member States for the opportunity and for the feedback and guidance. And I just want to also use this opportunity to just express my gratitude to Rector of UNU as the co-lead on this work package, but also in particular to the teams at the UN System Staff College, who with whom we have been engaged in a very constructive and collaborative process and also to the wider team of UN entities who are supporting this merger, recognizing that a key feature of this central learn engine will be about scale and speed and how through a networked approach, we're able to also support the efforts of our colleague entities across the system in driving capacity, not only of our own teams, but of institutions and/or public officials on the ground in countries. Thank you so very much, Mr. President.
I thank you also, ma'am, for your explanations. Finally, I give the floor to Mr. Ryder. You have five minutes.

Thank you.

I won't need five minutes, Chair, you'll be pleased to hear. Firstly, President, I think that this monthly briefing is proving its worth. I think this has been a very valuable exercise and we look forward to continuing it in the months ahead. We get a lot from it and I hope Member States also find it worthwhile. My colleagues Tom and Michel have responded, I think, to the specific issues addressed the work packages before us today and I hope replied effectively for the fellow briefing entities. So it remains for me only to make two rather general points, President. Firstly, it's encouraging for us to see that we've been able to convey to you the sense firstly of energy and then of joined-up-ness in the way that we are conducting our work under UNAT across different entities and across the entirety of the system. That momentum and collective effort is fundamentally important to making UNAT work. It does not happen by accident. I think the Secretary General is consistently, continually injecting the energy into our efforts by insisting that UNAT is and must remain a strategic priority for him. And it's also promoted by the way we're organised. We have a steering committee that brings together the different principles responsible for different areas of UNAT. I think that all of that promotes the collective effort that has been on display today, the coherence and the common purpose. I want to make one more general point. Many of you have reiterated the importance of provision of information. You want clarity on the process and progress that is being made. In my initial comments, I already presented to you the intention of the secretary general to provide consolidated information in a single report. We will be working on that in the future, but of course, that is not the only instrument. We have this briefing as an opportunity to share information, and each lead of each work package under UNAT is very clear that they have responsibility to inform member states and to consult with you as we go along, depending on the nature of the work package in question. That is all that I wanted to say. I thank all those who have participated in today's briefing. I think that it has proven to be extremely valuable, as I said just now. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. Ryder. And the formal meeting of the plenary is now concluded. I thank delegations for their participation. I think we have been quite efficient and the meeting is adjourned. Thank you. So there is no language.
